item.title: UK housing market remains subdued
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK housing market continues to show signs of subdued activity, according to the latest Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS) report. While some indicators suggest a gradual improvement in long-term sentiment, current conditions reveal stagnant buyer demand, declining house prices and ongoing challenges in the rental sector.

Market conditions remain challenging

Recent RICS data paints a picture of a housing market still struggling to gain momentum. Key findings include:

  • New buyer enquiries have remained largely flat across most UK regions
  • House prices continue their downward trend in many areas
  • The supply of rental properties remains constrained

These factors combine to create what many analysts describe as a "wait-and-see" market, with both buyers and sellers showing caution amidst ongoing economic uncertainty. The Bank of England's base rate decisions continue to influence mortgage affordability, potentially contributing to the subdued demand.

Glimmers of optimism emerge

Despite the current challenges, the RICS report does contain some positive indicators for the future of the UK property market:

  • Surveyors' 12-month price expectations have turned slightly positive
  • Long-term market sentiment shows gradual improvement
  • Certain regions are bucking the national trend with stable conditions

This cautious optimism suggests that while the immediate outlook remains challenging, many industry professionals anticipate a potential recovery further down the line. The rental market's supply issues may persist longer, with tenant demand continuing to outstrip available properties in most areas.

For those considering entering the property market, the current conditions present both challenges and opportunities. Mortgage borrowers might find it beneficial to compare deals carefully, as lenders continue to adjust their products in response to market conditions. Homeowners thinking of selling may wish to seek professional valuation advice to understand their local market's specific dynamics.

item.title: Listings outgrow sales agreed
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Recent data from July highlights a notable shift in the UK property market, with a growing number of listings outpacing agreed sales. This trend suggests a slower pace of deal conversions, alongside significant regional variations in market performance across Great Britain.

Increasing Property Listings

The latest figures reveal a rise in the number of properties being listed for sale. This increase in supply could indicate that more homeowners are choosing to put their properties on the market, potentially driven by factors such as changing lifestyle needs or economic conditions. However, whilst listings are on the up, the rate at which these properties are being sold appears to be lagging behind.

Slower Deal Conversions

Despite the uptick in listings, the conversion of these properties into agreed sales has been slower than anticipated. This could be attributed to a variety of factors, including buyer caution in the face of rising mortgage rates or uncertainty in the broader economic landscape. Borrowers might be taking more time to assess their options, leading to a delay in finalising purchases.

Regional Variations in Market Performance

The data also underscores significant differences in how the property market is performing across Great Britain. Certain regions may be experiencing more robust activity, with higher levels of sales agreed, whilst others could be seeing a more sluggish market response. Homeowners and potential buyers may wish to pay close attention to local market conditions, as these can vary widely and impact both saleability and pricing.

In summary, the July property market data paints a picture of growing supply but slower sales conversions, with notable regional disparities. For those considering entering the market, staying informed about these trends could be crucial in making well-timed decisions.

item.title: London prime sales rise and fall
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The London prime property market has shown mixed signals in recent months, according to the latest data from Knight Frank. Whilst transaction levels have strengthened, exchanges have weakened, and property values have experienced a decline. Meanwhile, the rental market continues to grow, presenting a complex picture for buyers, sellers, and investors alike.

Transaction Levels vs. Exchanges

Knight Frank’s report highlights a notable increase in transaction levels across London’s prime property market. This suggests that buyers are actively engaging with the market, potentially driven by shifting economic conditions or changes in mortgage rates. However, the data also reveals a contrasting trend in exchanges, which have weakened. This discrepancy could indicate delays in the completion process or hesitancy amongst buyers to finalise deals amidst ongoing market uncertainty.

Declining Property Values

The report points to a decline in property values within London’s prime market. This downward trend may reflect broader economic pressures, including higher interest rates and inflationary concerns, which could be dampening demand. Buyers in this segment might find opportunities to negotiate favourable terms, whilst sellers may need to adjust their expectations to align with current market conditions.

Continued Rental Growth

In contrast to the sales market, London’s prime rental sector continues to grow. The rise in rental demand could be attributed to factors such as increased flexibility amongst tenants, higher mortgage costs deterring potential buyers, or a growing preference for short-term commitments. Landlords and property investors may find this trend encouraging, as it suggests sustained demand for rental properties in the capital.

Overall, Knight Frank’s findings paint a nuanced picture of London’s prime property market. Whilst challenges persist in the sales sector, the rental market remains robust, offering opportunities for investors. Homeowners and buyers navigating this landscape may wish to carefully consider their options and seek professional advice to make informed decisions.

item.title: 1 in 8 new builds unsold after 6 months
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

New research reveals that approximately one in eight newly built properties across the UK remain unsold six months after completion, as developers focus on maintaining profit margins rather than reducing prices to attract buyers. With thousands of homes lingering on the market, this trend highlights potential challenges in the new-build sector amidst shifting market conditions.

Why new builds are staying on the market longer

Industry analysts suggest several factors contribute to extended selling periods for new-build properties. Many developers appear reluctant to adjust prices significantly, even when demand softens, preferring to wait for buyers willing to meet their target price points. This strategy helps protect profit margins but can result in slower sales cycles.

Other influencing factors include:

  • Regional variations in demand, with some areas experiencing particular oversupply
  • Changing buyer priorities post-pandemic, with some preferring older properties with more character
  • Competition from the second-hand market offering better value in some locations
  • Concerns about maintenance costs and service charges associated with new developments

What this means for prospective buyers

For those considering a new-build property, the current market conditions may present opportunities. Homeowners looking to purchase might find developers more open to negotiation on price or willing to include incentives after several months of unsuccessful marketing. Typical incentives could include:

  • Contributions towards stamp duty or legal fees
  • Upgraded fittings or appliances
  • Help-to-buy style schemes or part-exchange options

However, borrowers should carefully consider location and long-term value when evaluating new-build properties, particularly those that have been on the market for extended periods. While incentives can make a purchase more attractive, the fundamental aspects of the property and its surroundings remain crucial factors in any buying decision.

As the market continues to adjust, both buyers and developers may need to adapt their expectations. While some properties sell quickly, others may require more time to find the right buyer at the developer's desired price point, creating a varied landscape across different regions and development types.

item.title: Holiday let changes failing in Devon and Cornwall
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent reforms aimed at boosting residential property supply in Devon and Cornwall appear to be falling short of their intended impact, with sales growth in these regions continuing to lag behind wider UK markets. Despite policy changes targeting holiday lets, the anticipated shift towards more residential housing has yet to materialise.

Policy Reforms and Their Impact

Over the past year, the government introduced measures to address the growing issue of housing shortages in popular tourist areas like Devon and Cornwall. These reforms included stricter regulations on holiday lets and incentives to encourage the conversion of short-term rental properties into long-term residential homes. However, early data suggests that these changes have not significantly influenced the market dynamics in these regions.

The ongoing demand for holiday lets, coupled with the lucrative returns they offer, has meant that many property owners remain reluctant to shift their focus. This has resulted in a slower-than-expected increase in the availability of residential properties, leaving local buyers with limited options.

Market Performance in Devon and Cornwall

Whilst property markets in other parts of the UK have shown resilience and growth, Devon and Cornwall have struggled to keep pace. Sales volumes in these areas have remained subdued, with prices also experiencing slower growth compared to national averages. This discrepancy highlights the unique challenges faced by these regions, where tourism-driven demand continues to dominate the property landscape.

For prospective buyers, this situation may present both opportunities and obstacles. On one hand, slower price growth could make properties slightly more affordable. On the other, the limited supply of residential homes means competition for available properties remains high.

What This Means for Homeowners and Investors

For homeowners in Devon and Cornwall, the current market conditions may prompt a reassessment of their property strategies. Those with holiday lets might consider whether the ongoing returns outweigh the potential benefits of converting their properties to residential use. Meanwhile, investors looking to enter the market could find value in exploring opportunities that align with the long-term housing needs of local communities.

It could also be worth monitoring upcoming policy developments, as further reforms may be introduced to address the imbalance between holiday lets and residential housing. Staying informed about these changes may help buyers and investors make more strategic decisions.

As Devon and Cornwall continue to grapple with the challenges of balancing tourism and residential housing, the effectiveness of recent reforms remains under scrutiny. Homeowners and investors alike may wish to keep a close eye on market trends and policy updates to navigate this evolving landscape effectively.

item.title: When Co-Owners Can’t Agree on Selling Shared Property
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Shared property ownership can sometimes lead to disagreements when co-owners have different views about selling. Whether it's a family home, inherited property, or joint investment, disputes often arise when one party wishes to sell whilst the other prefers to retain ownership. These situations require careful navigation, as legal and financial implications may come into play.

Common Scenarios in Co-Ownership Disputes

Disagreements between joint property owners typically occur in several scenarios. Many involve former partners who purchased a home together but later separated, with one wanting to sell and the other refusing. Inherited properties can also cause friction when siblings or relatives have conflicting ideas about retaining or selling an estate. Similarly, investment properties owned by business partners may become contentious if one wishes to exit the arrangement and the other does not.

Differences in financial circumstances often fuel these disputes. One owner might need to release equity for personal reasons, whilst another may prefer to hold onto the property for long-term gains. Without clear agreements in place, these situations can become legally complex and emotionally charged.

Legal Options for Resolving Disputes

When co-owners cannot reach an agreement, the law provides several avenues to resolve the matter. Under English property law, joint tenants or tenants in common may apply for an order of sale through the courts. This legal process can force a sale if one party can demonstrate sufficient grounds, though it often involves time and expense.

Alternatively, homeowners might consider mediation services to negotiate an amicable solution without court intervention. Some co-owners opt for a buyout arrangement, where one party purchases the other's share at an agreed valuation. In cases where communication has broken down entirely, seeking independent legal advice becomes essential to protect individual interests.

It could be worth reviewing any existing co-ownership agreements or deeds of trust, as these documents may outline predetermined processes for handling disputes. Where no such agreement exists, parties may need to rely on statutory provisions to move forward.

Preventing Future Co-Ownership Conflicts

Prospective joint buyers might consider establishing clear terms before purchasing property together. A formal co-ownership agreement can specify how decisions about selling will be made, outline dispute resolution methods, and define each party's rights and responsibilities. These legally binding documents often prove invaluable if relationships between owners change over time.

For those already in shared ownership without formal arrangements, it may still be possible to create a deed of trust or similar agreement retrospectively. Consulting a property solicitor could help clarify options and potentially prevent future disagreements about selling shared assets.

Whilst shared property ownership offers many benefits, from financial advantages to emotional connections, these arrangements work best when all parties have aligned expectations. Taking time to establish transparent agreements from the outset could save considerable stress should circumstances change in future.

item.title: Agents now using AI to simplify AI-generated tenant complaints
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping the way the property sector operates, with letting agents now turning to the technology to manage a growing wave of AI-generated tenant complaints. Whilst AI tools can streamline processes and improve efficiency, they are also creating new challenges for agents who must navigate complex, detailed complaints drafted with the help of these programmes.

The Rise of AI-Generated Complaints

Industry experts have noted a significant increase in tenant complaints that are crafted using AI. Greg Tsuman, a former president of ARLA Propertymark, explained that AI can produce highly detailed, well-worded complaints that might previously have taken tenants considerable time and effort to compile. However, these complaints can sometimes lack merit or include inaccurate information, leading to potential complications for agents.

“AI tends to be user-biased,” Tsuman noted. “It can tell tenants what they want to hear, potentially creating a false sense of awareness about the validity of their complaint.” This has resulted in agents spending more time addressing intricate, multi-part complaints, even when they may not be grounded in fact.

How Agents Are Responding

To manage this influx of AI-generated correspondence, some letting agents are now using AI tools themselves. Tsuman’s company, for example, employs AI to summarise and analyse lengthy complaints, helping agents to identify the key points quickly. “AI doesn’t respond to complaints,” he clarified. “It assists with the heavy lifting, allowing us to focus on crafting a well-informed, human response.”

Ben Stokes, president-elect of ARLA Propertymark, has also observed this trend. He highlighted that AI-generated complaints often pull information from the internet, which can lead to misunderstandings or inaccuracies. “Agents need to carefully assess these complaints to ensure they address the genuine issues,” he added.

Calls for Transparency

Tsuman has suggested that it could be worthwhile for The Property Ombudsman to introduce rules requiring tenants to disclose whether AI was used to draft their complaints. “This wouldn’t prevent valid complaints from being raised,” he explained. “Instead, it would help to filter out spurious claims that might waste time and resources.”

By fostering transparency, agents could focus their efforts on resolving legitimate concerns, whilst tenants would benefit from clearer communication channels. This approach could strike a balance between leveraging AI’s capabilities and maintaining the human expertise essential to effective complaint resolution.

As AI continues to evolve, its role in the property sector is likely to expand further. For letting agents, embracing the technology whilst maintaining a critical eye on its outputs could be key to navigating this new landscape successfully.

item.title: Top line vanity, bottom line sanity
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Estate agency businesses often focus on headline fee income when discussing performance, but industry experts suggest cash flow and profitability tell the more important story. With rising fall-through rates and long transaction timelines, many agencies face financial pressures despite seemingly healthy turnover figures.

The reality behind estate agency finances

Whilst many agencies report strong valuation numbers and exchange volumes, the sector's fixed-cost structure creates significant financial challenges. Core expenses including branch leases, staff salaries, portal fees and regulatory costs remain constant regardless of transaction volumes. This operational gearing means even modest revenue declines can disproportionately impact profitability.

Industry observers note several recent profit warnings from major agencies, with concerns that more may follow. The time lag between sale agreements and completions - often spanning several months - exacerbates cash flow pressures. With fall-through rates now exceeding 25% in many cases, agencies incur substantial upfront costs that may never be recovered.

Why cash matters more than turnover

Professionals highlight three key financial metrics that tell different stories:

  • Fee income: The headline figure often discussed at industry events
  • Profit: What actually keeps the business operating
  • Cash position: Determines whether an agency can continue trading

The fixed-cost model creates what analysts describe as "brutal mathematics". Each pound earned above break-even contributes almost entirely to profit during good times, but the reverse applies during downturns. A 10% revenue decline might eliminate profitability entirely for some agencies.

Strategies for financial resilience

Industry experts suggest agencies could benefit from examining several areas:

  • Monitoring average fee percentages to identify discounting trends
  • Improving conversion rates at each transaction stage
  • Reducing fall-through rates through better transaction management
  • Reviewing ancillary income streams such as conveyancing referrals

Whilst the market presents challenges, the fixed-cost structure also means efficiency improvements flow directly to the bottom line. Careful financial management may help agencies navigate the current market conditions more effectively.

For homeowners, these industry dynamics highlight the importance of working with financially stable agencies that can support transactions through to completion, even in challenging market conditions.

item.title: Typical new build ‘contains £55,000 in hidden costs’
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Purchasing a new-build home in southern England could come with hidden costs averaging £55,000, according to recent findings from the Centre for Policy Studies (CPS). These additional expenses, often undisclosed to buyers, are attributed to various policy requirements such as affordable housing commitments and net zero targets. With the average new-build property priced at £450,000 in the region, homeowners may be unaware that a significant portion of this figure covers these embedded costs.

What Are These Hidden Costs?

The CPS estimates that approximately £50,000 of the average new-build price is made up of fees and charges not explicitly detailed to buyers. These include £10,000 for biodiversity net gain initiatives, which aim to enhance natural habitats, and £30,000 for planning obligations. The latter could fund affordable housing projects or local infrastructure improvements, such as road developments. Additional costs arise from planning fees and delays, further inflating the overall price. Alan Hibben, an Associate at the CPS, highlighted the opaque nature of these expenses, noting that they are often buried within the property’s price rather than being transparently communicated to buyers.

The Impact on Homebuyers

Hibben emphasised that these hidden costs are a direct result of policy decisions, with the financial burden being shifted onto homebuyers rather than being funded through general taxation. He argued that this approach allows governments to obscure the true costs of these policies, placing the blame on housebuilders instead. “Successive British governments have buried new taxes, fees and charges inside other systems, especially planning,” Hibben stated. This practice has created a housing market where public-policy costs are embedded in property prices, whilst political debates often focus solely on land, labour, and material expenses.

For prospective buyers, this lack of transparency could make it challenging to accurately budget for a new-build home. Whilst the allure of a modern property with energy-efficient features may be appealing, it could be worth factoring in these additional costs when considering affordability. Borrowers might also wish to seek independent financial advice to ensure they fully understand the financial implications of their purchase.

Looking Ahead

The CPS’s findings raise important questions about the fairness of embedding policy costs within property prices. As the government continues to pursue ambitious targets for affordable housing and environmental sustainability, the transparency of these costs remains a critical issue. Homeowners and buyers alike may wish to advocate for clearer communication of these expenses, ensuring they are fully informed when making one of the most significant financial decisions of their lives.

In conclusion, whilst new-build homes offer many advantages, the hidden costs associated with them could impact affordability for many buyers. Understanding these expenses and their origins is an essential step in navigating the complexities of the UK housing market.

item.title: Why letting agents are the cape-wearing heroes landlords need
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Private landlords in the UK face increasingly complex regulations, with recent legislation like the Renters' Reform Bill adding significant compliance responsibilities. Many property investors originally entered the market to build portfolios rather than navigate legal complexities, leading growing numbers to rely on professional letting agents to handle regulatory burdens.

The growing compliance challenge for landlords

Today's private rental sector operates within a detailed legal framework covering everything from deposit protection schemes and energy efficiency standards to electrical safety checks and eviction procedures. Recent changes have introduced stricter requirements around property conditions, tenant rights and documentation processes.

Key responsibilities now include:

  • Maintaining compliance with over 170 pieces of legislation governing rented properties
  • Keeping up with frequent regulatory updates including upcoming changes to Section 21 notices
  • Ensuring all safety certificates and property inspections remain current
  • Handling tenant disputes and deposit protections correctly

How letting agents can support landlords

Professional letting agencies offer comprehensive management services that could help landlords navigate this complex landscape. Their expertise typically includes:

  • Full legal compliance management, including staying abreast of legislative changes
  • Property marketing and tenant vetting services to help find reliable occupants
  • Rent collection and financial record-keeping
  • Coordination of property maintenance and mandatory safety checks
  • Handling of tenancy agreements, deposits and any disputes

For landlords with multiple properties or limited time, using an agent's services might prove particularly valuable. While this comes at a cost—typically 10-15% of monthly rent—many find the time savings and reduced regulatory risk justify the expense.

Property investors considering their options might wish to weigh the benefits of professional management against their own availability and expertise. With the regulatory environment showing no signs of simplifying, specialist support could help landlords focus on investment strategy rather than legislative detail.

item.title: How many home viewings before the stress kicks in?
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

House hunting can be an emotional rollercoaster for first-time buyers, swinging between excitement and anxiety within a single viewing. New research from property law firm LPL suggests there may be an ideal number of viewings before the process becomes overwhelming.

The tipping point for property viewings

The study indicates that most buyers begin experiencing significant stress after viewing around 10 properties. Whilst enthusiasm typically remains high during initial viewings, the cumulative effect of multiple property visits, financial calculations and decision-making can take its toll.

First-time buyers might consider pacing their viewings to avoid fatigue. Viewing more than three properties in a single day could lead to confusion rather than clarity, as distinguishing features between homes may become blurred.

Managing the emotional side of house hunting

Property purchases represent one of life's most significant financial commitments, so it's natural for emotions to run high. Buyers may wish to:

  • Take notes and photos during viewings to help recall properties later
  • Schedule viewings over several weeks rather than cramming them into weekends
  • Discuss impressions with a trusted friend or family member between viewings
  • Set realistic expectations about compromise and priorities

The research highlights how emotional fatigue can cloud judgement. Buyers who feel overwhelmed might benefit from taking a short break from viewings to reassess their criteria and financial position.

For those feeling the strain of property hunting, remembering that most buyers view an average of eight properties before making an offer could provide reassurance that the process takes time. Working with an experienced mortgage adviser may help streamline the financial aspects, allowing buyers to focus on finding their ideal home.

item.title: Platform links agents, lenders and conveyancers for quicker sales
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

A new digital platform aims to streamline property transactions by connecting estate agents, conveyancers, and mortgage lenders in a single workspace. PropTech firm myMoveToday has launched an AI-powered system designed to reduce delays and improve transparency throughout the homebuying process.

Cutting delays in property transactions

The platform targets one of the most common frustrations in property sales – the lack of visibility during conveyancing. By providing real-time updates on transaction progress and automated document tracking, the system could help reduce the average completion time for home purchases.

Early trials with London-based partners have reportedly shown promising results, with participants observing shorter completion timelines during pilot testing. The technology integrates with popular customer relationship management (CRM) systems used by estate agents, including Reapit, Alto, and Propertybase.

How the platform works

The system creates a shared digital workspace where all parties involved in a property transaction can collaborate. Key features include:

  • Chain visibility tools showing real-time progress updates
  • Automated document tracking and reminders
  • Integration with multiple CRM platforms
  • AI-powered workflow management

Steve Wanless, chief executive of myMoveToday, commented: "Estate agents often waste hours chasing updates because traditional conveyancing lacks transparency. Our platform brings all parties together, which could help reduce transaction failures and speed up completions."

For homeowners navigating the property market, such innovations might help reduce some of the stress associated with lengthy completion times. While no system can eliminate all delays, improved communication between agents, conveyancers, and lenders could potentially make the process smoother for all involved.

item.title: Industry mourns the loss of popular estate agent
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The property industry is mourning the loss of Tim O’Riordan, a well-known estate agent who co-founded O’Riordan Bond in 1995. Tim passed away last week at the age of 61, leaving behind a legacy of charisma, leadership, and a distinctive approach to estate agency that won him widespread admiration.

A Visionary in Estate Agency

Tim O’Riordan, alongside business partner Simon Bond, built O’Riordan Bond from a single Northampton branch into a thriving network of 15 offices across Northamptonshire, Milton Keynes, and Luton. The agency weathered the challenges of the 2007 financial crash and, under Tim’s guidance, doubled in size over the last three years, employing over 100 staff across sales, lettings, and mortgage services.

Simon Bond described Tim as a "one-off" whose magnetic personality and passion for the industry left a lasting impression. "Tim’s ability to light up a room was second to none," Simon said. "He was uncompromisingly himself, and clients, colleagues, and friends loved him for it." The agency’s early success was driven by Tim’s hands-on approach, focusing on face-to-face relationships and a strong local presence—a philosophy that remains central to the business today.

A Legacy of Fun and Community

Tim’s career spanned an era when estate agency was built on trust, personality, and a "work hard, play hard" ethos. Simon recalled the vibrant culture of the 1990s and early 2000s, before social media transformed the industry. "Tim led by example, making him a legend in Northamptonshire’s property scene," he said. "There are countless stories of his energy, humour, and dedication to both his team and clients."

After retiring in 2022 and relocating to Dorset, Tim remained closely connected to the business and took pride in its continued growth. His funeral, to be held on 21st August at East Coker Church in Somerset, is set to be a celebration of a life lived with enthusiasm, warmth, and an unmistakable flair.

Tim O’Riordan’s impact on the property industry—and the people who knew him—will be remembered for years to come. His legacy lives on not just in the business he helped build, but in the countless relationships he nurtured throughout his 30-year career.

item.title: Four out of five flats fail to sell within six months, says Zoopla
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New research from Zoopla has revealed that approximately 80% of flats across the UK fail to find a buyer within six months, highlighting significant challenges in this sector of the property market. The data suggests flats are facing weaker demand compared to houses, with complex leasehold arrangements and ongoing building safety concerns contributing to buyer hesitancy.

Why flats are proving difficult to sell

According to Zoopla's executive director Richard Donnell, while around half of all properties typically struggle to secure buyers, the figure rises dramatically for flats. Several factors appear to be deterring potential purchasers, including:

  • Uncertainty around service charges and ground rents
  • Ongoing concerns about cladding and building safety
  • The additional complexities of leasehold ownership
  • Lenders' increased caution when underwriting mortgages for flats

Donnell noted that freehold houses tend to attract more interest as buyers prefer having full control over their property without worrying about unexpected costs from third parties. The contrast is particularly stark in England, where leasehold arrangements are more prevalent compared to Scotland's share of freehold system.

The growing price gap between flats and houses

Zoopla's analysis shows the price difference between flats and houses has reached its widest point in thirty years. This divergence reflects changing buyer preferences and the additional risks associated with flat ownership. Prospective buyers are increasingly factoring in long-term costs like service charges and potential cladding remediation works when considering what price to offer.

Mortgage providers have also become more cautious, with many lenders implementing stricter criteria for flat purchases. This financial scrutiny, combined with buyer wariness, has created a perfect storm for flat sellers, many of whom find themselves waiting considerably longer to complete a sale than those marketing houses.

For homeowners looking to sell a flat, it could be worth getting professional valuation advice to set realistic price expectations from the outset. Some sellers might consider addressing any known building safety issues or obtaining relevant certificates before listing their property to improve marketability.

The current market conditions highlight the importance of thorough research for both buyers and sellers in the flats sector. With careful preparation and realistic pricing, transactions can still proceed, though perhaps not as quickly as sellers might hope in the current climate.

item.title: Rental homes in Manchester letting faster despite higher rents
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Manchester’s rental market is showing no signs of slowing down, with properties being let quicker than ever despite rising rents, according to recent research. The latest data reveals a competitive landscape for renters, driven by high demand and limited supply. This trend highlights the growing pressures faced by those searching for homes in the city.

Key Findings from the Latest Rental Report

The Manchester Rental Market Report, published by Rentaroof, indicates that the average rental property spent just 21 days on the market during the second quarter of 2026, down from 24 days during the same period in 2025. Notably, nearly 40% of properties were let within two weeks, with areas like Didsbury, Ancoats, and Chorlton-cum-Hardy among the fastest-moving markets.

Despite the speed at which homes are being snapped up, rents continue to climb. The average asking rent in Manchester rose by 2.7% year-on-year to £1,162. Rooms saw the steepest increase, with prices jumping by 10.4%, while flats and houses rose by 6.3% and 5.4% respectively. In the city centre, rents reached £1,356 per month, reflecting a 10.4% annual increase.

What’s Driving the Demand?

Experts attribute the intensifying competition to a combination of factors, including Manchester’s growing population, limited housing supply, and evolving rental legislation. The city’s universities, expanding job market, and thriving economy continue to attract new residents, but the pace of housing availability hasn’t kept up.

Jasper de Groot, CEO of Rentaroof UK, commented, “The imbalance between supply and demand remains the primary driver of Manchester’s rental market. Higher rents haven’t dampened the need for housing; instead, they’ve heightened competition, particularly for more affordable options. This is evident in the significant rise in room rents, as renters increasingly compete for budget-friendly accommodation.”

What Does This Mean for Renters?

For those searching for rental properties in Manchester, the market’s fast-paced nature means acting quickly is essential. Many renters are finding that delaying viewings or applications by even a few days can result in missing out on a property altogether. This urgency is particularly pronounced in sought-after areas and for lower-cost options.

With rents continuing to rise and competition intensifying, renters might consider prioritising their search criteria and being prepared to act swiftly when a suitable property becomes available. Additionally, exploring emerging neighbourhoods could provide more opportunities and potentially lower costs.

Manchester’s rental market shows no signs of easing, with demand outstripping supply and rents climbing steadily. For renters, staying informed and proactive could be key to securing a home in this competitive environment.

item.title: Prime Central London property prices have fallen 23% since 2015
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Prime Central London (PCL) property prices have experienced a significant decline since their peak in mid-2015, according to the latest data from Knight Frank. The report highlights a 23% drop in average prices over the past 11 years, driven by tax increases and political uncertainty. Despite modest gains in the two years leading up to April 2023, the market has struggled to recover from a prolonged downturn that began in June 2016.

A Decade of Decline

Knight Frank’s analysis reveals that average property prices in PCL fell by 3.3% in the year to July 2026, marking the 39th consecutive month of annual declines. When adjusted for inflation, the figures paint an even starker picture. UK CPI data shows cumulative inflation of 42% between mid-2015 and mid-2026, meaning a property purchased for £1 million in 2015 should theoretically be worth £1.42 million today. However, its actual value has dropped to £770,000, representing a 46% decline in real terms.

Tom Bill, head of UK residential research at Knight Frank, noted that while the summer of 2026 has seen a slight improvement in market activity compared to the previous year, the bar remains low. Transaction levels across London increased by 14% in the three months to July, with a modest 3% rise in PCL. This follows subdued activity in 2025, influenced by factors such as Donald Trump’s trade tariffs, the abolition of non-dom status, and speculation around property taxation ahead of the autumn Budget.

Market Challenges and Buyer Trends

The property market continues to face significant challenges, with the new government caught between conflicting pressures. A restrictive bond market limits spending, while Labour backbenchers oppose meaningful spending cuts. Additionally, the Labour manifesto has ruled out increases to income tax, VAT, or national insurance, leaving policymakers with limited fiscal options.

Compared to the five-year average, property exchanges are down 6% in London and 15% in PCL. However, these figures are skewed by stamp duty changes during and after the pandemic, as well as the sharp increase in mortgage rates starting in 2022. This makes it difficult to accurately assess the current strength of the market.

Buyers in PCL are also adjusting their priorities, with refurbishment projects gaining popularity. Stuart Bailey, head of prime central London sales at Knight Frank, explained that exceptional properties are in short supply, prompting buyers to consider homes that require renovation. This shift reflects a growing willingness to invest in potential rather than move-in-ready properties.

While the PCL market faces ongoing challenges, its long-term appeal remains intact. For homeowners and investors, staying informed about market trends and potential opportunities could be key to navigating this complex landscape.

This makes it difficult to accurately assess the current strength of the market.

Buyers in PCL are also adjusting their priorities, with refurbishment projects gaining popularity. Stuart Bailey, head of prime central London sales at Knight Frank, explained that exceptional properties are in short supply, prompting buyers to consider homes that require renovation. This shift reflects a growing willingness to invest in potential rather than move-in-ready properties.

While the PCL market faces ongoing challenges, its long-term appeal remains intact. For homeowners and investors, staying informed about market trends and potential opportunities could be key to navigating this complex landscape.

item.title: Mayor of London to fund Renters Rights Act enforcement officers
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

London Mayor Sadiq Khan has announced a £400,000 investment to bolster the enforcement of the Renters Rights Act and support tenants across the capital. The funding will focus on recruiting and training enforcement officers in boroughs throughout London, while also providing resources to organisations offering free advice and assistance to renters. This initiative aims to ensure tenants have access to support when facing issues such as unsafe housing conditions, unjust rent hikes, or landlords failing to comply with the law.

Addressing Housing Challenges in the Capital

With approximately 2.7 million Londoners renting privately, the city faces significant challenges in ensuring tenants have safe and secure homes. While many landlords adhere to regulations, issues such as damp, unsafe properties, and excessive rents persist. The new Renters Rights Act seeks to address these problems by strengthening tenants’ rights and offering greater security. However, for these rights to be effective, renters need to be aware of them and have access to support when disputes arise.

Mayor Khan emphasised the importance of this initiative, stating, “Every Londoner deserves a safe, secure, and decent home. This funding will help ensure the new rights for renters are more than just words on paper.” The investment is part of a broader effort to create a fairer housing market in London, where tenants can challenge rogue landlords without fear of jeopardising their tenancy.

Supporting Renters and Enforcing the Law

The £400,000 Renters Rights Enforcement Fund will be divided between training borough enforcement officers and supporting two organisations dedicated to assisting renters. These organisations will provide guidance and advocacy, helping tenants navigate disputes and seek justice when their rights are violated. Additionally, the training for council officers aims to ensure that the Renters Rights Act is effectively enforced, holding landlords accountable for any breaches of the law.

Mayor Khan highlighted the transformative potential of the Renters Rights Act, describing it as a “game changer” for tenants. He added, “These stronger rights and greater security will only make a difference if people know about them and can use them. This investment ensures renters have the support they need to challenge rogue landlords and secure justice.”

The initiative reflects the Mayor’s commitment to improving housing standards in London and creating a safer, fairer city for all residents. By empowering tenants and ensuring the Renters Rights Act is enforced, this funding represents a significant step towards addressing the challenges faced by renters in the capital.

item.title: Tenants need to earn £75,000 to rent in London
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

London renters now need to earn nearly £75,000 annually to afford the average rental property in the capital, according to the latest figures from Propertymark. This significant income requirement follows a 4.2% monthly rental increase, pushing average London rents to £2,484 per month.

Regional variations in rental affordability

While London dominates headlines with its steep rental costs, regional trends paint a more varied picture across the UK. The North West saw the second-largest monthly rent increase at 1.9%, taking average rents to £1,131 and requiring an annual salary of £33,930. Meanwhile, Wales bucked the trend with a 0.9% monthly decrease, bringing average rents down to £1,000 and reducing the necessary income to £30,000.

Other regions experiencing rent increases included:

  • West Midlands: +1.7%
  • South East: +0.8%
  • Scotland: +0.2%

Several areas saw modest monthly declines:

  • North East: -0.9%
  • East Midlands: -1.1%
  • South West: -0.7%
  • East of England: -0.2%
  • Yorkshire and Humberside: -0.1%

Market dynamics and expert commentary

Kim Lidbury, President of ARLA Propertymark, noted: "Rental markets continue to show considerable regional variation. While London leads with strong price growth, other areas maintain relative stability or see modest reductions." The 6.4% annual increase in London's salary requirement contrasts with Wales' 1.7% annual improvement in affordability.

The broader market continues to face fundamental supply challenges. Despite some moderation in growth rates compared to recent years, demand for rental properties significantly outweighs available supply across most regions. This imbalance maintains upward pressure on rents, particularly in high-demand areas like London and the North West.

Prospective tenants might consider their options carefully in the current market. While London remains particularly challenging, other regions offer more varied affordability. The data suggests that rental costs can fluctuate considerably between neighbouring areas, potentially creating opportunities for those with flexibility in their location choices.

item.title: Charity begins at home…with a home deposit
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Family financial assistance has become a crucial stepping stone for first-time buyers in today’s property market, according to new research. A study by The Private Office reveals that 97% of UK adults aged 45+ believe young people face significant hurdles purchasing property without family support, with 80% acknowledging homeownership is increasingly tied to intergenerational wealth.

The rise of the 'bank of mum and dad'

Property purchases now dominate family financial gifts, surpassing other forms of support. The research shows 51% of those who've provided monetary help did so specifically for property deposits, compared to 20% assisting with living costs and just 8% contributing to education. This shift reflects changing attitudes towards wealth transfer, with 81% believing financial support should occur during lifetimes rather than through posthumous inheritance.

Current gifting patterns reveal substantial sums changing hands: 22% of donors have given over £100,000, while 58% provided more than £20,000. Only 12% gifted less than £5,000. Interestingly, 82% opted for outright gifts rather than loans (12%), suggesting most families prefer unconditional support when helping relatives onto the property ladder.

Timing gaps in generational wealth transfer

While 71% believe financial support should come early when it can have maximum impact, HMRC data tells a different story. Those aged 85+ accounted for nearly 60% of estates reporting lifetime gifts in 2022/23, indicating wealth often transfers later than donors intend. This disconnect between intention and reality may leave younger generations waiting longer for crucial financial support.

Inheritance tax considerations appear less pressing than many assume - only 15% of estates with gifts incurred inheritance tax liabilities in 2022/23. However, with HMRC collecting £336m in inheritance tax from incorrectly structured gifts, families may wish to seek professional advice when planning substantial financial assistance.

As property affordability challenges persist, these findings highlight how family support has become embedded in the UK's homeownership landscape. With 88% of respondents open to helping younger relatives buy property, the 'bank of mum and dad' looks set to remain a key player in the housing market for years to come.

item.title: Renters’ Rights compliance simplified with Form 4A automation
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A leading property technology provider has streamlined the rent review process for letting agents by integrating the government's mandatory Form 4A directly into its platform. The move comes as the lettings sector continues adapting to requirements introduced by the Renters' Rights Act.

Simplifying rent increase administration

Since the legislation came into force, landlords and agents proposing rent increases on periodic tenancies have been required to use the official Form 4A notice. This previously involved multiple manual steps - downloading the form, re-entering tenancy details, arranging signatures and serving notices separately from customer relationship management (CRM) systems.

The new automated solution populates the form directly using existing tenancy data stored within the platform. Letting professionals can then review the document, make necessary amendments, apply electronic signatures and serve notices to tenants by email - all within a single workflow. Completed forms are automatically linked to the relevant tenancy records, creating a clear audit trail.

Built-in compliance for letting agents

The integration aims to reduce the administrative burden created by recent regulatory changes while helping agents maintain consistent processes when serving rent increase notices. Key features include:

  • Automatic population of tenancy, property and landlord details
  • Option to edit fields where required
  • Electronic signature capability
  • Multiple serving options including email delivery
  • Automatic document retention against tenancy records

Heather Staff, Co-CEO of Street Group, explained: "The Renters' Rights Act has brought important changes to the sector, but also created additional administration for what was traditionally a straightforward process. We believe compliance should be built into everyday workflows rather than becoming another manual task."

The functionality forms part of the company's existing lettings platform and is available within current rent review workflows at no extra cost to users. Agents retain flexibility in how they serve notices, with options to generate unsigned forms for alternative delivery methods if preferred.

This development represents another step in the digital transformation of the lettings sector, where technology providers are increasingly focusing on simplifying compliance through integrated solutions. As regulatory requirements continue evolving, such innovations may help letting professionals adapt more efficiently whilst maintaining full compliance.
